result:
I have a soft spot for unfinished things.

Half-read books with old receipts pressed between the pages. A sweater with one sleeve. The sentence a friend abandons halfway through because they're already laughing at the punchline they haven't said yet. Drafts, sketches, gardens that got a little ambitious in April and gave up by July.

There's something honest about them. A finished thing has to pretend it always knew where it was going. An unfinished thing admits it didn't.

Michelangelo left a series of sculptures called the *Slaves* — figures caught mid-struggle inside the marble, one arm free, the rest still stone. Art historians will tell you about technique and commissions falling through, but I like to stand in front of them (in my head, at least) and think they look more alive than most polished statues. They're not posing. They're becoming.

And we're surrounded by that kind of becoming, if you look for it. The Sagrada Família in Barcelona has been under construction for over 140 years, cranes as permanent a part of its silhouette as the spires. Siena tried to build a cathedral so big it would swallow the old one, ran out of money and plague years, and left one enormous, elegant wall standing alone. Now people picnic in its shadow. It's not a ruin, exactly. It's a cathedral that decided to be something else.

I think I love it because so much of modern life is weirdly obsessed with completion. Close the rings. Clear the inbox. Finish the season. Reach the end of the feed — as if there is one. Everything wants a checkmark.

But the best parts of a day rarely check anything off. It's the walk that wasn't exercise and wasn't errands, just a walk because the light was doing something interesting on the brick buildings. It's the conversation in a kitchen that drifts from dinner plans to childhood fears to whether ghosts would get bored, and never resolves any of it. It's learning three chords and noodling them badly on a porch for an entire summer instead of ever becoming "a guitarist."

My notebooks are full of ideas that stop mid-thought. A line of dialogue with no speaker. A map of a town that doesn't exist, but I labeled the bakery. A list titled "reasons to learn beekeeping" with only one item: *you get to wear the suit*. At first that felt like failure, all that potential squandered. Now I think of them as seeds with the wrapper still on. Not everything has to germinate on schedule.

Even bread knows this. You mix flour and water and wait, and most of the real work happens when you're not touching it at all. It rises in the quiet. If you keep poking it to check, you ruin the rise.

Maybe people are a little like that. We're constantly interrupting our own rising to ask if we're done yet.

So here's to the unfinished letter you'll probably never send but needed to write. To the language you learned just enough of to order coffee and say thank you like you mean it. To the novel in the drawer, the playlist that's only four songs long but perfect, the friendship that picked back up after two years like it was mid-sentence.

They aren't incomplete because they lack something.

They're open. And open things can still surprise you.
